doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

title: Assembling the NBC studio band and Carson
summary: He hired Severinsen, Clark Terry, Newsom, Haggart, Rosengarden and Pizzarelli, then did Today and Tonight shows under Allen and Carson.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: The musicians over the years that you’ve worked with in TV and in the studio have contained a lot of our best jazz musicians.

Well that was the home factory. Because as the band business, as we talked about, began to dissipate, a lot of these men had no place to go except to play in theaters and at that time it was sin to play a pit job, it really was strange—

—how the philosophy changes. Now it’s the elite job in New York. But at that time, they really didn’t want a staff job either. It was strange. They didn’t know where to go or what to do. So I brought men like, well I could start with Doc Carl Severinsen. I took him from Charlie Barnet’s band, and Clark Terry from the Ellington band, Tommy Newsom was with the Navy band in Washington, Hymie Schertzer had been with the Goodman band, I mean I could go through the whole, Bobby Haggart of course of fame, the best bass player I’ve ever known in my life, and Bob Rosengarden, who pretends that he never played with Henry Bussey but he did.
I’ll tell him that. You actually referred to him as the Chairman of the Board of the Time Factory.

And Bucky of course I knew from the Vaughan Monroe Orchestra. So it wasn’t me, I had a commitment to change the style of the orchestra and to do that, you know you have to start from scratch and I was so fortunate to have these type of players who still had enthusiasm for playing. And then one of my jobs was to do the service shows, The Today Show and The Tonight Show. I mean I did specials, but The Tonight Show, I was stuck in the pit for a long time. And then having Steve Allen, who loved this and was learning to play piano. And then I must say when Carson came aboard, he didn’t want me there. He wanted somebody else, because I was the house man. So he looked upon me as a sort of spy you know, naturally. That’s the psychology of our business. And for a couple of years it was this smiling beautifully on camera and total silence off. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
